extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, USPTO officials, and legal/economic researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical assessment of how patent examiners use prior art (applicant- vs examiner-submitted citations), implications for patent validity, disclosure duties, bibliometrics, and policy reforms. Focuses on issued U.S. patents and citation-use in rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (statutory rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections of the patent statute and their associated rejection types: Section 101 (non-patentable subject matter), Section 102 (lack of novelty), Section 103 (non-obviousness), Section 112 (written description/enablement), and Section 121 (restriction requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 shows the share of patents receiving different types of rejections by art unit. These statutory categories are the substantive legal benchmarks against which prior art is evaluated during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner consideration of prior art (presumption of consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal presumption that a patent has been examined over all relevant prior art (and thus is valid) rests on the assumption that examiners actually considered the cited art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues the presumption is questionable because much cited art—especially applicant-submitted art—was not substantively used in prosecution. It suggests limiting the presumption of validity to art the examiner actually discussed substantively during prosecution, not merely to art listed on the face of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of applicant-submitted versus examiner-cited references
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a cited reference (patent or non-patent literature) was originally provided by the applicant or added by the examiner affects the likelihood it was used in a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: applicant-submitted references are far less likely to be used in rejections than examiner-cited references (Table 4: e.g., applicant references used ~2% overall vs examiner references used ~39.5%). This is a practical criterion for measuring whether citations were operational in examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of applicant submissions relative to docket/office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether applicant-submitted prior art arrives before docketing, after docketing but before the first office action, or later can be used to assess whether applicants were tailoring claims ex ante or merely supplying art post-filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data: ~22% of applicant-submitted U.S. patent references and 17% of foreign patent references arrive after initial claims were submitted (post-docket, pre-office action). Models show no significant difference between later and earlier arriving art overall and for some types of prior art, which undermines the hypothesis that applicants systematically draft around their own cited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance indicator via EPO X/Y classification
rubrics_metrics.description: References designated X or Y on EPO search reports are likely to be materially relevant to patentability and thus serve as an external relevance signal for citations that later appear in U.S. prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among late-arriving applicant patent citations, those flagged as X/Y on corresponding EPO reports are modestly more likely (~10 percentage points higher) to be used by U.S. examiners than other late applicant cites, although they remain substantially less likely to be used than examiner-found art (e.g., still ~26 percentage points less likely than examiner-cited U.S. patents). Sample sizes are small, so interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-of-applicant-art hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis that applicants predominantly submit low-quality or irrelevant prior art, which would explain examiner non-use of applicant citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from EPO-identified relevant cites undermines this hypothesis as a complete explanation; some applicant-submitted art is objectively relevant yet still not used by U.S. examiners. Nonetheless, low applicant search effort or ignorance could still contribute in part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner myopia / salience and time-constraint explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may focus on art they find themselves due to cognitive bias (overvaluing what they find) or time constraints, leading to underuse of externally provided art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors identify myopia and time pressure as the most plausible explanations for the observed gap. Policy reforms that merely increase external art provision (worksharing, peer-to-patent, outsourcing) may fail unless they also increase the salience of outside art to examiners or change examiner incentives, training, or evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy intervention options to improve prior-art discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible reforms include requiring applicants to conduct searches, requiring applicants to explain the relevance of submitted prior art, outsourcing search to professionals, implementing worksharing with foreign offices, or strengthening inequitable conduct rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and practical constraints exist: there is currently no statutory requirement to search or to explain relevance (PTO attempted a rule in 2006 but withdrew it after litigation and comments). The paper cautions against relying solely on disclosure requirements or inequitable conduct because data do not support that applicant art is uniformly poor and because inequitable conduct rules can cause overcompliance and litigation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication for duty of candor / inequitable conduct enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The normative and enforcement implications of the finding that applicant-submitted art is often not used by examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiners ignore much submitted art, then withholding art may have little practical effect on patent scope, suggesting courts and policymakers may be over-emphasizing inequitable conduct sanctions tied to nondisclosure. The paper notes, however, inequitable conduct may still matter for non-art information (e.g., misleading assertions of unexpected results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining 'consideration' of prior art in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: How courts should treat a cited reference when assessing whether the PTO 'considered' that art (relevant post-Microsoft v. i4i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: define consideration as more than mere listing of a reference on the patent face; litigation standards should allow parties to argue that cited art was present but likely not substantively attended to by the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on sample selection — issued patents only
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses are based on issued patents and therefore may not capture cases where applicant-submitted prior art caused rejections and subsequent abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors acknowledge possible selection: if applicant art leads to provisional rejections and abandonment, issued-patent sample underestimates the practical effect of applicant-submitted art. Thus inferences should be limited to issued patents unless further work addresses prosecution outcomes including abandoned applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of citation counts in patent bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions behind using forward and backward patent citations as indicators of patent 'quality', 'importance', or 'impact' rely on the idea that citations were vetted and reflect meaningful examination or influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: substantial noise exists because many applicant citations were not used in rejections and many examiner practices focus primarily on U.S. patents. This calls for caution in interpreting citation-based metrics; violation of the 'carefully vetted' assumption could add noise or bias, and the exact effect on common measures is unclear.
